The trailhead stood at the end of a gravel road that wound through stands of lodgepole pine, and by the time the four of them arrived the light had begun to thin. Mara had packed the maps, Jonah carried the stove, and the others divided the food between their packs. They had planned the trip for months, checking forecasts every evening, comparing routes, arguing about mileage, and reading old journals that described creek crossings and snowfields in exhausting detail. None of them had expected the gate to be locked.

A laminated notice explained that the road beyond the gate was closed for repairs and that hikers should park at the lower lot and walk an extra two miles. Jonah studied the map while the others tightened their straps. The detour would add distance but not much climbing, and the weather was still holding, so they started down the shoulder of the road anyway. The first mile passed quickly. The second was slower. The packs settled, the conversation faded, and the forest closed in on both sides of the path.

Late in the afternoon they reached a ridge where the trees thinned and the whole valley opened below them, gray and green and folded like a blanket. They stopped to drink water and eat the last of the bread. A cold wind came up the slope, carrying the smell of rain. Mara watched the clouds pile against the far peaks and did her best to guess how much daylight remained. The map showed a lake another three miles ahead, and beyond it a pass that would take them down to the road on the far side. If the weather turned, the pass would be the wrong place to be.

They reached the lake just as the first drops fell. The water was black and smooth, and the far shore disappeared into mist. Jonah pitched the tent while the others gathered what dry wood they could find under the trees. For a while nobody spoke. Then Mara crouched by the small fire, holding her hands out to the warmth, and said, 'We shouldn't have waited so long at the trailhead. We didn't bring enough water, and I wouldn't want to run out up here.' Jonah nodded slowly. 'We couldn't have known the gate would be locked,' he said. 'But you're right. We shouldn't have counted on the lake, and I don't think we should stay past morning.' The wind shook the tent all night, and by dawn the clouds had swallowed the pass completely.
